en.body:
## The Secret Phrase That Unlocked a Universe

The second episode of **Lanterns** might not feature **Hal Jordan** and **John Stewart** in their iconic green uniforms for extended periods, but it's packed with enough comic book depth to satisfy the most dedicated fans. Beyond a mention of the dreaded **Manhunters** and John Stewart wielding his power to create a construct, the episode reveals a fascinating detail about how Green Lanterns store their power sources: in pocket dimensions. This practice, a staple since the Silver Age of comics thanks to creators like **John Broome** and **Gil Kane**, adds a layer of practical, almost whimsical, technology to the Corps.

However, the standout moment for eagle-eyed viewers was the passphrase **Hal Jordan** used to grant **John Stewart** access to his personal dimension. As John approached the hidden access point, Hal declared, "Mogo doesn't socialize." This isn't just random dialogue; it's a direct, exhilarating reference to the title of a seminal short story by the legendary **Alan Moore** and **Dave Gibbons**, the creative minds behind **Watchmen**. The story "Mogo Doesn't Socialize" first appeared in 1985's *Green Lantern* #188 as part of the *Tales of the Green Lantern Corps* backup series, a period that saw significant expansion and deepening of the Green Lantern mythology.

## A Nod to a Comic Masterpiece

The Green Lantern Corps itself was a major innovation, transforming the concept of the Green Lantern from a singular hero, like the Golden Age **Alan Scott** with his magical ring, into an intergalactic peacekeeping force. The introduction of **Hal Jordan** in 1959's *Showcase Comics* #22 marked the beginning of this expansive universe, overseen by the **Guardians of the Universe**. Broome and Kane were instrumental in building this universe, quickly introducing characters like **Tomar-Re** in 1961. The choice to echo Moore's story, which itself explored the isolation and unique nature of the sentient planet and Green Lantern, Mogo, suggests the showrunners are keenly aware of the rich, often philosophical, history of the Corps and are eager to bring its most compelling elements to life.

## What's Next

This Easter egg is more than just a fun callback; it signals a show that respects its comic origins and is willing to explore the complex character dynamics and lore that have made the Green Lanterns enduring figures. Fans can anticipate further deep dives into the established history of the Corps as **Lanterns** continues its run, with future episodes likely to unpack more hidden gems and character-defining moments.

content_raw: This article contains spoilers for Lanterns season 1 episode 2. We still aren’t getting many scenes of Hal Jordan and John Stewart in green tights, but the second episode of Lanterns has a lot of comic book weirdness. Not only do the Manhunters get a mention and John makes a construct, but we also see a lantern tucked away in a pocket dimension. Hal and his fellow GLs have been keeping their lanterns in pocket dimensions since John Broome and Gil Kane have been telling their stories in the early Silver Age. But the most exciting reference might be the passphrase that Hal uses to give John access to his pocket dimension. When John walks up to the box that hides access to the dimension, he lifts up the phone and asks Hal to speak. “Mogo doesn’t socialize,” declares Hal. That answer doesn’t just open the box, it also excites comic book fans in the audience, who know that phrase as the title of a classic story by Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons, the creative team behind Watchmen . “Mogo Doesn’t Socialize” appears in 1985’s Green Lantern #188, as part of series of back-up stories called Tales of the Green Lantern Corps . The Green Lantern Corps were one of the innovations that Broome, Kane, and editor Julius Schwartz made when they reinvented the Green Lantern concept for the Silver Age. The original, Golden Age Green Lantern was Alan Scott, a man who made a magical wishing ring out of a meteorite that fell to Earth. 1959’s Showcase Comics #22 introduced Hal Jordan as the latest recruit into the Green Lantern Corps, a set of intergalactic peacekeepers who worked for the Guardians of the Universe. Broome and Kane quickly began developing the Green Lantern Corps, introducing fellow members such as Tomar-Re in 1961’s Green Lantern #6 and Katma Tui in 1964’s Green Lantern #30, as well as Corpsman-turned-villain Sinestro in 1961’s Green Lantern #7. However, the other members of the Corps never got much attention until the 1981 miniseries Tales of the Green Lantern Corps by Mike W. Barr, Len Wein, and Joe Staton, and even that still had Hal Jordan front and center. Starting in 1982 with Green Lantern #148, back-up stories introduced readers to other members of the Green Lantern Corps, often weird aliens with wildly different backstories. The anthology format meant writers could experiment with the Green Lantern concept, which drew the attention of Alan Moore, who would do some of his best DC Comics work in his three Green Lantern Corps stories. “Tygers” in Green Lantern Corps Annual #2 explains why Hal Jordan’s predecessor trusted a spaceship instead of his ring, creating a horror tale about the hellish planet Ysmault and introducing the Daxamite Green Lantern Sodam Yat.
